items.title: Today's lesson
items.content:
A boy who hardly needs the toilet after a hot cricket match, and **gum** oozing from a babool tree, open the lesson: how do living things get rid of harmful wastes?

Students follow **urine** from the kidney to the urethra, then follow blood through a **nephron** to see urine formed by **filtration** and **selective reabsorption**.

An **artificial kidney** does the same cleaning by diffusion alone, and the lesson ends with how **plants** get rid of waste.

Some pictures have a **second picture or animation**: show picture 1, ask, then click ›.

items.title: You already know
items.content:
• arteries carry blood to an organ, veins carry it away, and capillaries have walls one cell thick

• substances diffuse from where they are more concentrated to where they are less concentrated

• plants lose water vapour through their stomata (transpiration)

items.title: By the end, you can
items.content:
**1.** Describe the human excretory system.

**2.** Describe the structure of a nephron and explain how urine is formed.

**3.** Explain the principle of an artificial kidney in one or two lines.

**4.** Describe how plants get rid of waste.

**5.** Label a diagram of the excretory system and a nephron.

chunks.name: A hot match and a babool tree

items.text:
**What this shows**

Left: on a **hot day**, Arjun gulps water after batting, sweating hard.

**Answer to Question 1**

Take guesses and leave it open. On the hot day he loses a lot of water as **sweat**, so his kidneys keep back more water and make **less urine** (Part 2).

**What this shows**

Right: **gum** oozes from a babool tree; grandmother collects it. Yellow leaves are falling.

**Answer to Question 2**

Take guesses and leave it open. **Yes**: plants store wastes as **gums and resins** in old xylem, and in leaves that **fall off** (Part 4).

items.text:
**Step 1: start here**

Read the key idea: harmful nitrogen wastes such as **urea**; removing them is **excretion**. Then reveal the figure (pointer 2).

**Step 2: picture 1 of 3**

Point out the two **kidneys**, the **renal artery** bringing blood in and the **renal vein** taking it away. The names along the urine path are hidden (?). **Do not click › yet.**

**Answer to Question 3**

**Step 3.** The **renal artery**: the kidney removes urea, so the blood in the renal vein is cleaner.

**Answer to Question 4**

**Step 4.** Kidney → **ureter** → **urinary bladder** → **urethra**. Now click › on the figure to check (pointer 5).

**Step 5: click › (now 2 of 3)**

After Question 4. The hidden names appear: **ureter**, **urinary bladder**, **urethra**. Check the order from Question 4 on the figure.

**Answer to Question 5**

**Step 6.** The **urinary bladder**: it is muscular and **stretches** to store urine. When it is full we feel the urge, and we control when it is emptied: it is under **nervous control**. Now click › to see the whole flow (pointer 7).

**Step 7: click › (now 3 of 3)**

After Question 5. The flow: blood with urea enters by the renal artery and leaves clean by the renal vein; then urine runs down the **ureters**, the **bladder** fills and stretches, and the urine leaves by the **urethra**. A caption names each step.

*Picture 2 is animated: it plays on its own and repeats. Click **‹** to return to picture 1 and stop it.*

items.prompt: In this excretory system, which part carries urine from a kidney to the bladder?
True or false? “The urethra carries urine from the kidneys to the urinary bladder.”
options: False: the renal veins do this
False: urine is made in the bladder

items.text:
**On this question**

**A**: **B**, the ureter. All the parts: A kidney, B ureter, C urinary bladder, D urethra, E renal artery, F renal vein.

**On this question**

**A**: the **ureters** carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder; the urethra carries it out of the bladder.

items.text:
**Step 1: start here**

Read the key idea: about **a million nephrons** in each kidney. Then look at one nephron (pointer 2).

**Step 2: picture 1 only**

Follow one nephron: blood arrives in a **branch of the renal artery**, enters the **glomerulus** inside **Bowman’s capsule**; the **tubule** winds through **capillaries** to the **collecting duct**. **Do not click › yet.**

**Answer to Question 6**

**Step 3.** **Water, glucose, amino acids, salts and urea** pass through; **blood cells and proteins** are too big and stay in the blood. Now click › on the figure (pointer 4).

**Step 4: now click ›**

After Question 6. Picture 2 (legend bottom left) shows three stages, each with a caption: **filtration** into Bowman’s capsule, **selective reabsorption** back into the capillaries, and **urine** flowing down the collecting duct.

*Picture 2 is animated: it plays on its own and repeats. Click **‹** to return to picture 1 and stop it.*

items.text:
**Step 1: picture 1 of 3**

Blood arriving in a branch of the renal artery. Use the legend: blood cells, proteins, water, glucose and amino acids, salts and **urea**.

**Step 2: click › (now 2 of 3)**

**Filtration**: in the glomerulus, the small substances pass into Bowman’s capsule as **filtrate**. Blood cells and proteins are too big and stay in the blood.

**Step 3: click › (now 3 of 3)**

**Selective reabsorption** along the tubule: glucose, most water and most salts go back into the blood. What is left (mostly urea) is **urine**.

**Step 4**

Read the key idea, pointing back to each box of the figure.

**Answer to Question 7**

**Step 5.** It is **reabsorbed** into the blood; otherwise we would lose litres of water and all our glucose every day.

**Answer to Question 8**

**Step 6. Less**: the body has extra water, so more is left in the tubule, giving a lot of **dilute urine**. Question 1 from the hook is now answered: on the hot day, Arjun lost water as sweat, so **more** was reabsorbed.

items.prompt: In this nephron, in which part is the blood filtered, and in which is glucose taken back?
Healthy urine has no glucose. Why does glucose appear in the urine when blood sugar is very high?
options: Too much is filtered to reabsorb all

items.text:
**On this question**

**A**: filtered in **A**, the glomerulus (into B); glucose taken back in **C**, the tubule. All the parts: A glomerulus, B Bowman’s capsule, C tubule, D collecting duct, E branch of renal artery, F branch of renal vein.

**On this question**

**A**: so much glucose is **filtered** that the tubule cannot **reabsorb** all of it, so some is left in the urine.

items.text:
**Step 1: start here**

Read the key idea: when kidneys fail, an **artificial kidney** cleans the blood.

**Step 2: picture 1 only**

Trace the blood: from an artery, through the **pump**, along the long tubes in the **tank**, and back to a vein. Fresh fluid comes in; used fluid goes out. The magnified circle is hidden (?). **Do not click › yet.**

**Answer to Question 9**

**Step 3.** Urea **diffuses** from the blood (a lot) into the fluid (none). Glucose and salts are equally concentrated on both sides, so there is **no net movement**. Now click › on the figure (pointer 4).

**Step 4: now click ›**

After Question 9. Picture 2: in the magnified circle, **urea** (dots) crosses the lining from the blood into the fluid one by one, **glucose and salts** (squares) stay equal on both sides, and **blood cells** stay in the blood. The picture is only a depiction: the number of dots is not a real count.

*Picture 2 is animated: it plays on its own and repeats. Click **‹** to return to picture 1 and stop it.*

**Answer to Question 10**

**Step 5.** There is **no reabsorption**: wastes simply diffuse out. A kidney filters everything small, then takes back what is useful.

items.prompt: Why must the dialysing fluid keep being replaced with fresh fluid?
options: Urea builds up, so diffusion stops
The glucose in it runs out

items.prompt: **Assertion (A):** Dialysing fluid contains glucose. **Reason (R):** Glucose in the fluid stops glucose diffusing out of the patient’s blood.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A.
Both are true, but R does not explain A.
A is true, R is false.
A is false, R is true.

items.text:
**On this question**

**A**: urea collects in the fluid; once the fluid has as much urea as the blood, urea stops **diffusing** out.

**On this question**

**(a)**: with equal glucose on both sides, there is no net loss of glucose from the blood.

items.text:
**Step 1: start here**

Read the key idea: plants have **no excretory organs**. Then reveal the tree (pointer 2).

**Step 2: picture 1 only**

Five magnified circles: a **stoma** in a leaf, **falling leaves**, a leaf **cell**, the **bark**, and the **roots** in soil. Their names are hidden (?). **Do not click › yet.**

**Answer to Question 11**

**Step 3.** Through the **stomata**, by diffusion; extra **water** leaves the same way, as water vapour (transpiration). Carbon dioxide also diffuses out.

**Answer to Question 12**

**Step 4.** Many plant tissues are **dead cells**, and the plant later **sheds** its old leaves and bark, taking the wastes with them. Question 2 from the hook is now answered. Now click › on the figure (pointer 5).

**Step 5: now click ›**

After Question 12. Picture 2: the names appear and each circle lights up in turn: bubbles leave the stoma, old leaves fall, gum drips from old xylem, wastes in a vacuole, wastes going into the soil.

*Picture 2 is animated: it plays on its own and repeats. Click **‹** to return to picture 1 and stop it.*

items.prompt: A neem tree sheds many leaves before spring. How does this help it excrete?
options: Wastes stored in the leaves go too

items.prompt: Which two wastes leave a leaf through the stomata?

items.text:
**On this question**

**A**: wastes stored in the old leaves are removed when the leaves **fall off**.

**On this question**

**A**: **oxygen** (by day) and **water vapour**. Other wastes are stored in **vacuoles**, in falling leaves, or as **gums and resins** in old xylem.
